newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Militant Sunnis burn Iranian centre in Lahore.
newsitem.headline: Militant Sunnis burn Iranian centre in Lahore.

text.p: Sunni Moslem militants, angered by a bomb blast that killed their leader and 25 other people, set fire to an Iranian information centre in the Pakistani city of Lahore on Sunday, witnesses said.

Saturday's bombing, which Sunni hardliners blamed on Iran and the local Shi'ite Tehrik-i-Jafria Pakistan (TJP) group, raised fears of sectarian unrest just two weeks before Pakistani elections on February 3. The TJP has condemned the blast.

The witnesses said activists of the Sipah-i-Sahaba Pakistan (SSP) group attacked and burned the Iranian centre in a two-storey building in central Lahore. People were evacuated from upper-floor offices. There were no reports of casualties.
Thousands of people watched earlier as the body of SSP leader Zia-ur-Rahman Faruqi was taken through the city, and many joined prayers for him at a mosque on the main Mall Road.
The fire gutted the information centre and spread to adjacent shops on Mall Road as firemen battled the blaze.
Iranian diplomats in Islamabad could not immediately be reached for comment on the attack.

Faruqi was killed in a bomb blast outside the Sessions Court in Lahore on Saturday, shortly before he and his deputy Azam Tariq were due to appear on charges of involvement in the sectarian murders of a score of Shi'ites.
The official news agency APP quoted police as saying the bomb death toll had climbed to 26, including 19 policemen, while 25 of about 90 wounded remained in critical condition.

Faruqi was due to be buried on Monday in his home town of Samundri, about 300 km (187 miles) south of Islamabad. Tariq, who survived a grenade and rocket attack in 1994, was seriously wounded and APP said one of his legs had been shattered.
The remote-control bomb, apparently left on a motorcycle, went off shortly after noon as Faruqi and Tariq arrived at the court to be greeted by supporters showering them with flowers.
President Farooq Leghari condemned the bombing as "a dastardly act of terrorism".

No group has claimed responsibility for the attack. It appeared to be the latest in a long-running feud between militants in Pakistan's majority Sunni and minority Shi'ite communities, which cost about 170 lives last year.
Shi'ites form about 15 percent of Pakistan's population of over 130 million, but are a majority in neighbouring Iran.
The secretary of Iran's National Security Council, Hassan Rowhani, urged Islamabad last week to crack down on what he called terrorist groups and prevent killings of Shi'ites.
"The groups not only endanger Pakistan's security but also hamper the unity of Moslems," Rowhani, a Shi'ite cleric, told visiting Pakistani Foreign Minister Sahibzada Yaqoob Khan.
The SSP issued a statement on Friday calling the Iranian statement interference in Pakistan's internal affairs.
On Sunday, newspapers quoted a spokesman from the Sunni group as saying that Iran was providing Shi'ite groups with guns and money.
"We have been warning the government about Iranian backing for the Pakistani Shi'ite community," he said.
Shi'ite militancy in Pakistan was fuelled by the 1979 Islamic revolution in Iran, sparking a fierce backlash from well-armed Sunni groups such as the SSP.
